summary: Hamed and Maziar from LinkedIn AI present 360Brew, a foundation model for personalized ranking and recommendation. Current recommendation systems suffer from disjoint optimization, task-specific training, and slow rollouts. The team built a 150-billion-parameter LLM-based model with three key characteristics: zero-shot capability for new tasks, in-context learning for cold-start users, and instruction following so users can express their interests. The pipeline involves 'promptification' of user data, continuous pre-training, fine-tuning, alignment, and step-by-step distillation down to a ~3B model for production. The go-big-then-go-small recipe is essential: small models trained from scratch underperform. Three quality levers improve results: data scaling, model size scaling (Mixture of Experts from 7B to 8x22B), and context length. Results show improvements on cold-start users and out-of-domain tasks versus task-specific production models. Serving requires handling tens of thousands of QPS with sub-second latency. Efficiency levers include gradual step-by-step distillation (150B→3B→1B), gradual pruning (aggressive pruning causes up to 1% quality loss), mixed-precision quantization (FP8 for activations and parameters but FP32 for the LM head to preserve calibration), and attention sparsification enabling multi-item scoring of up to 500 items simultaneously. Over 4-5 releases, latency was reduced 7x and throughput increased 30x. Q&A reveals 50-60 benchmarks for measuring generalization, chronological ordering of user history as sufficient for most applications due to freshness bias, and a highly automated experimentation system pushing results automatically into spreadsheets.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: 360Brew is a 150B-parameter LLM-based foundation model for all LinkedIn personalization and ranking tasks, distilled step-by-step down to ~3B then 1B for production serving
The 'go big then go small' recipe is essential: gradual step-by-step distillation from 150B through intermediate sizes is far more effective than direct distillation
Gradual pruning and distillation cycles preserve quality; aggressive pruning at the start causes up to 1% quality loss
Mixed-precision quantization uses FP8 for activations and parameters but requires FP32 for the LM head to maintain calibration and distinguish between recommended items
Attention sparsification enables multi-item scoring of up to 500 items at once without items attending to each other, using custom kernels in SGLang and vLLM
Over 4-5 releases, latency was reduced 7x and throughput per GPU increased 30x
360Brew shows growing advantage over production models for cold-start users and matches or beats task-specific models on out-of-domain tasks
Generalization is measured with 50-60 internal and external benchmarks including IFEval, with tasks never seen in training data
Chronological ordering of user history works well for most applications due to recommendation systems' freshness bias, though balancing positive/negative distribution in context remains a challenge
Heavy automation in the training and experimentation pipeline is critical; results are pushed automatically to spreadsheets, enabling efficient parameter tuning

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.summary: Hamed introduces the problem: recommendation systems are deeply integrated but suffer from disjoint optimization, task-specific training, and slow rollouts. The mission is to build one LLM-based foundation model with a holistic understanding of the user journey to solve all LinkedIn personalization tasks.

sections.title: Three Desired Model Characteristics
sections.summary: The model must have zero-shot capability for new surfaces without data collection, in-context learning for cold-start users, and instruction following so members can tell the model their interests. Maziar takes over to explain model building.

sections.title: Model Building: Promptification and Pipeline
sections.summary: Maziar explains promptification—converting user data into structured prompts. The training pipeline goes from open-source model through upcycling, continuous pre-training, fine-tuning, instruction fine-tuning, and alignment to produce 150B-parameter Blue XL, then distills to ~3B for production. Automation across the pipeline is critical. Going big first then distilling small is essential; small models from scratch underperform.

sections.title: Levers for Model Improvement
sections.summary: Three levers improve quality: data scaling (more user data improves performance), model size scaling (7B to 8x22B Mixture of Experts increases performance), and context length (more user history improves performance, though drops at very long contexts due to model generalization limitations).

sections.title: Results: Cold Start and Generalization
sections.summary: Results show 360Brew's advantage over production models grows for cold-start users with fewer interactions, leveraging world knowledge. For four out-of-domain tasks never seen in training, 360Brew matches or beats task-specific production models, enabling faster surface rollouts.

sections.title: Serving Challenges and Efficiency Levers
sections.summary: Hamed introduces serving challenges: recommendation systems require tens of thousands of QPS and sub-second latency. Three efficiency levers are specification, smaller models via distillation, and quantization. The recipe is go big then go small via step-by-step distillation from 150B through 3B to 1B. Gradual pruning with distillation cycles is far more effective than aggressive pruning, which causes up to 1% quality loss.

sections.title: Quantization and Attention Sparsification
sections.summary: Quantization uses FP8 for activations and parameters but requires FP32 for the LM head to preserve calibration and item distinguishability. Attention sparsification prevents items from attending to each other during multi-item scoring, enabling up to 500 items per query. Over 4-5 releases, latency was reduced 7x and throughput increased 30x.

sections.title: Q&A: Generalization, Context Management, and Automation
sections.summary: Q&A covers measuring generalization with 50-60 benchmarks including IFEval, multi-item scoring implementation using custom kernels in SGLang and vLLM with attention masking, chronological ordering of user history as sufficient due to freshness bias, the challenge of balancing positive/negative distribution in context while preserving KV caching, and a highly automated experimentation system that pushes results automatically to spreadsheets.

limitations: Model performance drops at very long context lengths due to poor generalization of the architecture, not because information is less informative
The 150B Blue XL model cannot serve online due to QPS and latency constraints
Small models trained from scratch do not perform well; distillation from a large teacher is required
Aggressive pruning at the beginning significantly degrades quality; gradual pruning-distillation cycles are necessary
FP8 quantization on all layers significantly hurts performance; FP32 is required for the LM head to preserve calibration
Smarter context ordering beyond chronological is complicated by the need to preserve KV caching in serving
No out-of-the-box recommendation foundation model exists for smaller companies; this gap motivated the 360Brew project
Balancing positive and negative distribution within the context remains an ongoing ML engineering challenge
